paragraphs: The paper exercise shows whether you are willing to check drawing revisions, gauge status and deviations. Workplace authorization, actual inspection and release are separate decisions.

Machinists turn metal into acceptable precision parts under drawings and process requirements: interpreting part drawings and engineering information, selecting machining methods and sequences, calculating dimensions and tolerances, using micrometers, vernier calipers, and other gauges, setting up and operating lathes, milling machines, shapers, or grinders, programming CNC equipment when needed, monitoring feeds and speeds, measuring and inspecting finished parts against specifications, maintaining machines, and assembling and aligning fixtures and tools.

Try M01 in the entry section. Check the fictional diameter and length readings for A, B and C, then repeat with revision v2. Write a handoff that identifies the pending drawing, the deviations and what must not be released.
Consider this work if you like reading drawings, repeating measurements and recording evidence, and you will pause when a drawing or gauge is unresolved. Use interests to decide what to explore next.

This guide follows U.S. O*NET 51-4041.00. Machinists read drawings, set up machine tools, make precision parts, check tolerances, and record deviations. They may also program CNC tools or maintain equipment. U.S. pay and employment use the separate machinist occupation. Compare mainland China roles by the machines they use and the work they deliver.

entries: Work inputs: metal materials and blanks, part drawings and engineering information, dimension and tolerance requirements, machine tools such as lathes, mills, shapers, and grinders and CNC systems, fixtures and cutting tools, gauges such as micrometers and vernier calipers and inspection standards, process flows, and inspection records.

Checkable outputs: parts machined to tolerance, setup and alignment records, CNC programs, first-article and in-process inspection records, conformity and nonconformity determinations and corrective records, and machine maintenance records.

Full workflow: interpret drawings and process requirements → select machining methods and operation sequences → clamp and align work and set up machines and tools → trial cut and inspect the first article → machine and monitor feeds and speeds → measure and inspect against specifications → maintain machines and record inspection and correction results.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether methods and sequences are appropriate, how to select datums and workholding, how to meet tolerance and surface requirements, when first-article and in-process results are nonconforming, and whether deviations require parameter adjustment, rework, or scrapping.

Environment and pace: mainly on-site machine-shop work. Most respondents wear protective equipment daily, continuously use their hands on tools and controls, stand while working, and have relatively fixed schedules. Accuracy is extremely important; equipment speed affects the pace, with time pressure, hazardous equipment, and noise exposure.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest codes, education, and Job Zone information from O*NET 51-4041.00. Wage, employment, and industry data cover this occupation. Findings do not establish mainland Chinese qualifications, pay, or employment definitions.

Check first: part drawings and tolerance requirements, machining processes and sequences, workholding and datums, gauges and inspection methods, machine and tool condition, protective requirements, and nonconformity handling and recordkeeping requirements.

Work cycle: start with drawing interpretation and process selection, proceed through workholding and alignment, machine setup, trial cuts and first-article inspection, machining and process monitoring, then measurement, inspection and determination, maintenance records, and corrections. Do not begin batch machining until first-article and safety conditions are confirmed.

Machinists have a separate U.S. statistical classification, but may use lathes, mills, or grinders and may write CNC programs. Mainland China lists lathe and milling occupations by their equipment and tasks. Their duties can overlap.

CNC programmers write and optimize CNC programs and process documents. Machinists set up and operate machines, clamp and align work, and perform precision inspections. They often collaborate but have different authorization and outputs.
Tool and die makers fabricate and repair tooling, dies, and special tools. Machinists focus more on machining and inspecting general precision parts; tooling and dies are only part of their tasks.

Mainland China lists lathe work (6-18-01-01) for surfaces of revolution and milling (6-18-01-02) for surfaces such as flats and grooves. Both include CNC trades. U.S. machinists may use either type of machine; a mainland posting does not map directly to the U.S. occupation.

Welding and brazing equipment operators handle welding and joining processes. Machinists focus on cutting, dimensional tolerances, and precision inspection; joining processes have different machining boundaries.

Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can interpret drawings and handle dimensional tolerances patiently, stand and operate with focus for long periods, measure and inspect under procedures and record truthfully, and accept responsibility for machining accuracy and safety. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses; they cannot replace real task experience.
Positive signals: understanding drawings and tolerances, sequencing operations by datums and processes, patient measurement and review, and adherence to safety and equipment procedures.

Conditions for caution: unwillingness to verify tolerances and datums, difficulty maintaining precision under equipment pace and time pressure, a tendency to skip first-article inspection, or inability to follow protective and equipment safety requirements.

Trial action: independently calculate M01 dimension intervals and compare the three parts, listing unresolved items such as Q1 calibration / material / datums. Another person's calculation check is optional. Being within range on paper does not authorize real inspection release.

The RIASEC interest code is RCI (Realistic—Conventional—Investigative): a preference for hands-on machine-tool operation, precise machining under procedures, and analyzing process problems. These labels describe activity preferences only; they cannot determine competence or qualifications.

This round obtained no personality validity studies for machinists. Use M01 paper dimensions and unresolved-item records to observe verification habits. Paper results within range do not equal real inspection release or safety fitness.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications; they may only support self-reflection.

Entry paths and capability stages

For U.S. machinists, BLS lists a high school diploma or equivalent, no prior work experience in a related occupation, and long-term on-the-job training as typical. An apprenticeship is one option. Check equipment, training, and authorization with the employer.

China lists lathe operators (6-18-01-01) and milling operators (6-18-01-02) separately, with CNC variants in each. U.S. Machinists 51-4041 covers a wider range of machines. Compare the equipment and process in the specific role.

Verify training records, skills certificates, equipment operation authorization, and legally required special-operation certificates separately. First verify actual tasks and local applicable rules; a US certification entry point cannot establish Chinese certificate types or requirements for all workers.

Entry stage: practice drawing interpretation, gauge use, simple-part machining, and first-article inspection records under supervision, learn process and safety procedures, and retain process records.

You may first submit M01's four paper deliverables to demonstrate truthful dimension comparisons and unresolved-item records. They do not prove actual machining or inspection ability, which requires authorized training and competency assessment.
Ask which machine is used, whether you write programs, who checks the first part, and who owns the gauges and deviations. Check the role’s certificates, equipment authorization and applicable rules.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, handle complex parts and CNC programming, instruct new workers, and contribute to process improvements, or move into tool and die making, quality inspection, and production management.

Changde’s May 26, 2026 issue lists 17 CNC lathe positions at Hunan Teli Hydraulics. It asks for secondary vocational education or above, familiarity with the controls, programming and independent operation. It quotes CNY 7,000–11,000 per month on piece rate.

The April 8, 2026 Miyun job fair lists two CNC lathe roles at the Beijing Research Institute of Extraction and Application Technology, with junior college education. The row gives 4,700–9,000 without a pay period, so it cannot be reported as monthly pay. Both examples are historical, not national wages or current vacancies.

career_risk_cards.boundary: Final process and quality handling is determined by employer procedures, equipment requirements, and applicable regulations. This page does not replace safety procedures or professional advice.
career_risk_cards.direct_answer: Risks must be handled in terms of triggers, consequences, controls, and escalation boundaries.
career_risk_cards.evidence_scope: Check guarding separately from energy control during servicing. U.S. 1910.212 addresses machine guarding; 1910.147 covers applicable servicing with unexpected start-up or stored-energy hazards. Use the site’s authorized rules and local requirements.
career_risk_cards.heading: Machinists' Work Risks and Boundaries

risks.consequence: May cause machinery and cutting-tool injuries.
risks.mitigation: Do not start or continue using the machine. Stop work and report under site procedures. Personal protective equipment does not replace machine guarding.
risks.scenario: When a machine guard is missing, faulty, or bypassed.

risks.consequence: May cause out-of-tolerance dimensions and scrapping.
risks.mitigation: Verify datums and inspect the first article before machining.
risks.scenario: When machining begins without verifying datums and parameters.

risks.consequence: May cause deviations and safety hazards.
risks.mitigation: Clamp by datums and review fastening.
risks.scenario: When workholding or alignment is insecure.

risks.mitigation: Review drawings and confirm with process staff.
risks.scenario: When drawings or processes are misinterpreted.
When protection is absent around noise or hazardous equipment.

risks.consequence: May cause batches of scrap and safety problems.
risks.mitigation: Stop hazardous work and report under site procedures. If clearing a blockage or servicing exposes workers to unexpected startup or stored energy, authorized personnel verify energy control under the applicable procedure. A stop button does not isolate energy. Do not bypass guards.
risks.scenario: When machining continues despite tool wear or equipment anomalies.
risks.title: Handling equipment or tool anomalies without stopping
